teaser: Her first owner lived with her for years, then sent her back for a new face.
review_notes:
Repainting of the face (Fanny Cornforth replaced by Alexa Wilding) in 1872-73 at Leyland's request: standard account, please confirm dates.
Watercolor replica of 1867 in the Metropolitan Museum showing Cornforth's features: please confirm.
White roses supplied from John Ruskin's garden (reported by Rossetti's assistant H. T. Dunn): fairly sure, please confirm.
Flower meanings (white rose, poppy, foxglove) follow the usual Victorian readings.
Bancroft purchase after Leyland's death in 1892 and gift to Delaware by his family in 1935: please confirm.
Quoted line from the sonnet 'Body's Beauty': 'one strangling golden hair'.

lesson.text: The first person to own this painting kept it for a few years, then sent it back to the artist. Frederick Leyland, a Liverpool shipping magnate, had no complaint about the hair, the roses or the subject. He wanted a different face. In 1872 Dante Gabriel Rossetti scraped out the head and painted another woman onto the same body.

The original face belonged to Fanny Cornforth, Rossetti's housekeeper, model and lover: round-cheeked, earthy, a little amused. The replacement is Alexa Wilding, a dressmaker he had spotted in the street and hired for her cool, regular features. So the woman you see is a composite. The body and the famous hair were painted for one model, the face for another.

You can still meet the first Lilith. In 1867 Rossetti made a watercolor copy of the picture, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, and nobody ever asked him to change that one. It shows Fanny Cornforth's features.

Lilith comes from Jewish legend. She is the first wife of Adam, made before Eve, who refused to obey him and left Eden. Later stories turned her into a demon who preys on men. Rossetti gives her no wings, no snake and no ancient costume. He sits her in a modern bedroom in a white gown, doing something completely ordinary.

lesson.title: What she is doing
lesson.text: The whole action of the picture fits in three places.

spots.title: The comb
spots.text: She draws a comb through a long hank of hair held out at arm's length. The gesture is slow and lazy, and it displays the hair like goods on a counter.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Heavy eyelids, a full red mouth, a long neck. Her eyes slide down and to the left. She does not look at us, and she never will.

spots.title: The hand mirror
spots.text: This is what she is looking at. We get only the black back of the mirror. Her reflection is for herself alone.

lesson.text: That self-absorption is the danger. Rossetti wrote a sonnet to go with the painting, and in it Lilith's hair is a net. A young man looks, and she leaves “one strangling golden hair” wound around his heart. In Victorian England, where respectable women pinned their hair up, hair worn loose like this was a private sight, close to undress.
Rossetti's Lilith is frightening because she needs nobody. The painting makes indifference, not wickedness, the mark of the dangerous woman.

Now try to work out the room. There is a chair, a dressing table, a wall of roses pressing in from behind. Top left, a patch of sunlit green trees seems to offer a way out, a window onto a garden. Check it again. The candles in front of it are a clue.
That leafy view at the top left is not a window. What is it? Tap it.

spots.title: A mirror, not a window
spots.text: It is a swivel mirror on the dressing table, with a candle on each side. The trees are a reflection of a garden that must lie somewhere behind us, or nowhere at all.

lesson.text: So the only outdoors in the picture is an image in glass, and some see in it a memory of Eden. Everything else is shut in. There is no floor, no far wall, no air. Roses, fur, hair and skin are packed against the surface like a tapestry. Rossetti had no interest in a believable room. He wanted a rich pattern you cannot step back from.

The roses were painted from real blooms. Rossetti's studio assistant recalled being sent to fetch great basketfuls of white roses from the garden of the critic John Ruskin, an early champion of the Pre-Raphaelite painters.

Victorians read bouquets the way we read emoji. A whole “language of flowers” gave each plant a meaning, and Rossetti chose his with care. He also threaded one color through the cream and gold as a warning. Wander around and collect the reds.

spots.title: White roses
spots.text: Roses stood for love, and white ones for a love that is cold. A legend says every rose in Eden was white until Eve arrived and they blushed.

spots.title: The poppy
spots.text: One red poppy sits in a glass in the bottom corner. Opium comes from poppies, so the flower meant sleep, forgetting and death.

spots.title: Foxgloves
spots.text: Pink foxglove bells lie on the dressing table. The plant is poisonous, and in the language of flowers it stood for insincerity.

spots.title: The scent bottle
spots.text: A pink glass bottle with a gold stopper, the equipment of the dressing table. Beauty here is something worked at, with tools.

spots.title: A red band
spots.text: A coral-red ribbon circles her wrist, the same red as her lips. A tasseled cord of the same color trails across her lap.

spots.title: A wreath in her lap
spots.text: A garland of pale flowers tied with ribbon rests on her knees, perhaps meant for her hair once the combing is done.

lesson.text: Rossetti planned a partner for this canvas: Sibylla Palmifera, a calm woman holding a palm branch. He named the pair in two sonnets, Body's Beauty for Lilith and Soul's Beauty for the other. It says something that people remember the body. Painters and poets of the next thirty years filled their work with her descendants, the so-called femme fatale, the beautiful woman who destroys.

After Leyland died in 1892, the painting was bought by Samuel Bancroft, a cotton-mill owner from Wilmington, Delaware, who had fallen for Pre-Raphaelite art on a trip to England. His family gave his collection to the Delaware Art Museum in 1935.

Leyland got the face he asked for, and the picture lost something Rossetti's friends had admired in the first version: warmth. Whether the colder Lilith is the better Lilith is still argued over. Legend's most disobedient woman ended up repainted to suit a customer.

quiz.question: What did the first owner ask Rossetti to change?
quiz.explanation: Frederick Leyland had the face of Fanny Cornforth replaced with that of Alexa Wilding.

quiz.question: Who is Lilith in legend?
quiz.explanation: In Jewish legend she was made before Eve, refused to obey Adam and left Eden.

quiz.question: What is the leafy view at the top left of the painting?
quiz.explanation: It is a swivel mirror on the dressing table, flanked by candles.

quiz.question: What did the red poppy stand for?
quiz.explanation: Opium comes from poppies, hence the link with sleep and death.

quiz.question: In Rossetti's sonnet, what does Lilith leave around a young man's heart?
quiz.explanation: The sonnet describes “one strangling golden hair” wound around his heart.

facts.text: In the painting, Lilith looks straight at the viewer.
facts.explanation: She looks only at her own reflection in the hand mirror.

facts.text: A watercolor copy of the picture still shows the first model's face.
facts.explanation: The 1867 watercolor in New York was never repainted and shows Fanny Cornforth.

facts.text: Rossetti paired this painting with another called Sibylla Palmifera.
facts.explanation: The two stood for Body's Beauty and Soul's Beauty.
